A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support, unless a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R2. If no multiple support agreement is mentioned, assume there is none.
R3. A qualifying child must be the taxpayer's child, stepchild, placed foster child, brother or sister, or a descendant of one of them (such as a grandchild, niece or nephew).
R4. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year.
R5. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R6. If the return does not say someone else can claim the taxpayer, assume no one can.
R7. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R8. A taxpayer who can be claimed as someone else's dependent may not claim any dependent.
R9. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R10. A qualifying relative may not be the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.
R11. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more). This rule does not apply if the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
